newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. council raps Libya for sanctions-busting flight.
newsitem.headline: U.N. council raps Libya for sanctions-busting flight.

text.p: The Security Council rapped Libya on Friday for a recent flight by a Libyan aircraft from Tripoli to Saudi Arabia in defiance of U.N. sanctions connected with the 1988 bombing of a Pan Am airliner over Lockerbie, Scotland.

It marked the third year in a row that Libya violated the sanctions by flying pilgrims to Jeddah on an unauthorised flight even though the council gave permission for an Egyptian airline to ferry Libyans wishing to make the annual pilgrimage to Mecca.

In addition to an air embargo, the sanctions included a ban on arms sales and a downgrading of diplomatic relations. They were imposed in 1992 because of Libya's failure to extradite two men charged in Britain and the United States with involvement in the mid-air bombing of Pan Am flight 103, which killed 270 people.
A statement read at a brief public meeting said the Security Council considered "this clear violation ... as totally unacceptable" and called on Libya to "refrain from any further such violations."

The council recalled that "arrangements have been made consistent with" the sanctions regime "in order to fly Libyan pilgrims to perform the Haj" (pilgrimage). This was a reference to the 45 return flights the council authorised EgyptAir to make between Libya and Saudi Arabia to accommodate some 11,000 pilgrims.
The statement was almost identical to one issued by the council after last year's sanctions violation.
Libya has said in the past that pilgrims do not need U.N. authorisation to perform their religious duties.

The council said it would review the matter if further violations occurred and asked its sanctions committee to draw the attention of all U.N. members to their obligations if a Libyan-registered plane landed in their territory. In that case, the aircraft is supposed to be impounded.
Libya also violated sanctions in January by flying an official delegation to Accra, Ghana, and back. The U.N. sanctions committee has asked Libya for an explanation.
